title: The wonder stuff: What happened to graphene?

The wonder stuff: What happened to graphene?

What is graphene?

First isolated in 2004 by University of Manchester professors Andre Geim and Kostya Novoselov by repeatedly sticking and peeling away adhesive tape from a block of graphite (the same stuff found in pencils), graphene is a single, one-atom-thick layer of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb-like lattice. 

It is hundreds of times stronger than steel and up to five times stiffer than carbon fibre, yet is able to stretch by up to 20% its length. It can be folded, rolled or wrinkled; it’s also a supremely good conductor, up to 70% more electrically conductive than copper and up to 2.5 times more thermally conductive than diamond, considered to be one of the best conductors of heat. 

Graphene’s range of applications is huge, from computer chips and energy storage to paint and tennis rackets, so little surprise the professors received the Nobel Prize for Science in 2010, and little surprise it arrived in cycling a few years later to much fanfare.

Why was graphene touted as being the next big thing in bikes? 

‘Its strength-to-weight ratio, stiffness and energy-damping properties suggested it could make carbon fibre bikes lighter, stronger, more durable and more comfortable, especially when used as an additive to improve the performance of composite materials,’ says Ivan Buckley, director of the Graphene Engineering Innovation Centre at the University of Manchester. 

Emiliano Sabetti, director of product development at Vittoria, which uses graphene in its tyres, agrees, albeit he’s keen to keep expectations realistic: ‘If properly mixed into the carbon fibres and resin, graphene could enhance the molecular bonding and therefore the stiffness and the ultimate strength of a part. Nevertheless, in this field the expected gains are really marginal.’

Did any of this come to fruition?

Graphene had a moment in bike frames in 2016, when British brand Dassi released the Interceptor carbon race bike that had graphene added to boost stiffness and lower weight. The result was a 750g frame, but what really grabbed the public imagination was Dassi’s assertion that this new tech placed 350g frames in reach. Sadly the Interceptor never achieved mass production and Dassi folded in 2020. 

So was it all marketing nonsense?

‘Expectations were ahead of reality,’ says Buckley. ‘Graphene’s potential hasn’t fully materialised because it’s typically used in very small amounts, is difficult and costly to manufacture, and is being added to already highly optimised materials. So while it delivers real benefits, they are targeted and incremental rather than transformative.’

Sabetti adds, ‘Graphene is very expensive. There are technical challenges in the mixing process as well as in the balance of the formulation that require years of research and development to get graphene’s benefits into the final product.’

Do any cycling products successfully use graphene?

Yes, Vittoria thinks so. It first mixed graphene into its tyre compounds in 2015 to harness its reinforcing and heat-conductive properties. 

‘This achieves compound formulations that overcome the trade-off between rolling resistance, grip and durability,’ says Sabetti. 

‘It’s also used in some carbon components such as wheels and still occasionally in bike frames,’ says Buckley. ‘It’s used in brake pads and performance clothing, where it’s added to improve grip, durability, heat management and life span.’

One such example is clothing brand Givelo’s cycling kit.

‘We mix graphene into our Italian fabric to make a polyester and graphene blend,’ says Givelo co-founder Steven Dennis. ‘Being significantly more electrically conductive than copper, it makes a durable but flexible fabric for cycling that maximises temperature regulation.’

Will graphene’s place in cycling change in the future?

‘Niche and high-end brands can justify the cost and complexity,’ says Buckley, ‘so you’ll see more graphene in premium tyres, wheels and occasionally frames, where marginal gains matter and marketing value is high. 

‘In the mass market, cost, scalability and proven benefit dominate, so graphene only appears where it’s cheap and clearly effective, such as in tyre compounds. Otherwise it’s often skipped or used in very small amounts. So the trajectory isn’t just about the material improving, it’s about whether the performance gain is big enough to justify the cost at each price tier.’
